common_name: Alabama Blackeye Butterbean (Alabama Black Eye Lima Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm, above 65°F; Alabama Blackeye is a vigorous, long-vining pole type that needs a tall, sturdy trellis or fence, often reaching 10 feet or more.

directions: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun after soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F, training the long twining vines up a tall, sturdy trellis, fence, or row of poles. Alabama Blackeye is a family-passed-down Alabama heirloom baby lima, also known regionally as a butterbean, bearing small, creamy white seeds marked with a distinctive small black eye at the hilum. It is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant and keeps setting pods heavily through the hottest, muggiest stretches of Gulf Coast summer that slow many other lima varieties, making it a reliable choice for zone 9a gardens. Pick pods at the green shell stage for fresh eating in classic Southern butterbean dishes and succotash, or let pods dry fully on the vine for storage; shell beans regularly to keep the vigorous vine productive into fall.

common_name: Violet's Multicolored Butterbeans (Multicolor Speckled Pole Lima Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil is thoroughly warm, above 65°F; a vigorous semi-bush to pole type that readily tops a 7-foot pole and benefits from sturdy trellising.

directions: Direct sow seed 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil in full sun once soil temperatures stay reliably above 65°F, providing a sturdy trellis or pole for the vigorous semi-bush vines, which will readily top a 7-foot support and can reach 10 feet. This Georgia family heirloom, preserved for four generations by Violet Brady Westbrook's family in Banks County, produces 3-5 inch pods filled with small, richly flavored seeds displaying a striking rainbow of colors — cream, beige, red-brown, and violet-purple, swirled and speckled so that no two beans look quite alike. Plants show good disease and drought resistance, useful traits for humid Gulf Coast summers. Pick pods at the green shell stage for fresh butterbeans or let them dry fully on the vine for long-term storage; the colorful seed coats fade somewhat with cooking but the flavor remains excellent fresh or dried.
